title: Qualitative and Mixed Methods – What a Quantitative Researcher Must Know

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Qualitative research studies meanings, experiences and processes through words and observation rather than numbers, asking how and why rather than how many. Mixed-methods research combines qualitative and quantitative data in one study and integrates them at the design, methods or interpretation stage (Fetters et al., 2013).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
A survey can tell you that 40% of infants are not exclusively breastfed. It cannot tell you why mothers give water in the first month, who advises them, or what an ASHA’s message sounds like at the doorstep. Those questions need qualitative methods, and the answers often decide whether a quantitative intervention works.

The logic of sampling differs. A quantitative sample is chosen to represent a population so that estimates generalise. A qualitative sample is chosen for information: purposive sampling selects people who can speak to the question (recall §6.3.2), and theoretical sampling chooses the next participants to test ideas emerging from the analysis so far. Sampling stops at saturation, when new data stop yielding new codes or themes. In a systematic review of empirical tests, saturation was reached within 9–17 interviews or 4–8 focus group discussions, “particularly those with relatively homogenous study populations and narrowly defined objectives” (Hennink & Kaiser, 2022). Treat these as a planning range, not a rule.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Three data-collection methods recur in community medicine:

Method What it is Use it for
In-depth interview (IDI) One participant, open questions from a topic guide Personal experience, sensitive topics
Focus group discussion (FGD) A small group of similar participants led by a moderator Shared norms, community language, range of views
Key informant interview (KII) One person chosen for position or expertise (a medical officer, an anganwadi supervisor) How a programme or system works

Thematic analysis is “a method for identifying, analysing and reporting patterns (themes) within data” (Braun & Clarke, 2006). Its six phases: (1) familiarising yourself with your data; (2) generating initial codes; (3) searching for themes; (4) reviewing themes; (5) defining and naming themes; (6) producing the report (Braun & Clarke, 2006). A theme is not decided by counting: “The ‘keyness’ of a theme is not necessarily dependent on quantifiable measures – but rather on whether it captures something important in relation to the overall research question” (Braun & Clarke, 2006).

Rigour is judged by trustworthiness rather than validity and reliability: “Quality criteria for all qualitative research are credibility, transferability, dependability, and confirmability” (Korstjens & Moser, 2018). Credibility (are the findings believable? checked by triangulation, comparing data sources or methods, and member checking, taking findings back to participants), transferability (thick description so readers can judge fit to their setting), dependability (an audit trail of decisions) and confirmability (findings grounded in data, with the researcher’s reflexivity, an account of how their own position may have shaped the data, stated).

Mixed-methods designs (Fetters et al., 2013):

  • Convergent: collect both at the same time, analyse separately, compare.
  • Explanatory sequential: quantitative first, then qualitative to explain the results (a survey finds low IFA adherence; IDIs with non-adherent women explain why).
  • Exploratory sequential: qualitative first, then quantitative to build or test (FGDs generate items for a new questionnaire, then validated as in Chapter 16).

points.html: Report qualitative studies with COREQ (a “32-item checklist for interviews and focus groups”, Tong et al., 2007) or SRQR (21 items, O’Brien et al., 2014).
Qualitative findings are not generalised statistically; their transferability is judged by the reader from the description of setting and participants.
Do not add p-values to qualitative counts, and do not treat an FGD’s majority view as a prevalence.

questions.prompt: Name the reporting guideline for each: (a) a cluster-randomised trial of weekly iron–folic acid in schools; (b) a case-control study of neonatal sepsis; (c) the accuracy of a digital haemoglobin meter against the laboratory; (d) a systematic review of yoga for hypertension; (e) FGDs with ASHAs on home visits; (f) a risk score predicting pre-eclampsia.
questions.answer: 1. CONSORT, with its extension for cluster trials. (b) STROBE. (c) STARD. (d) PRISMA. (e) COREQ (or SRQR). (f) TRIPOD+AI, which supersedes TRIPOD 2015 (§17.4).

questions.prompt: Rewrite for a results section: “Not exclusively breastfed infants had significantly more diarrhoea (χ² = 23.37, p < 0.001).” Use the numbers of §10.6.4.
questions.answer: “Diarrhoea occurred in 33 of 80 infants (41.3%) who were not exclusively breastfed and 14 of 120 (11.7%) who were, a risk ratio of 3.54 (95% CI 2.02 to 6.17; χ² = 23.37, p < 0.001).” The effect and its interval come first; the test statistic and p-value follow, if given at all.

questions.prompt: A district survey finds that only 35% of pregnant women took 100 IFA tablets. The team then interviews 15 women who did not, choosing them to include different ages, parities and blocks, and stops when new interviews add no new reasons. Name the mixed-methods design, the sampling approach and the stopping rule.
questions.answer: Explanatory sequential design (quantitative first, qualitative to explain it). Purposive sampling, with maximum variation across age, parity and block. Stopping at saturation, when new data yield no new codes or themes; 15 in-depth interviews lies within the 9–17 range at which empirical studies reached saturation for fairly homogeneous groups (Hennink & Kaiser, 2022).
